deadlines.deadline: Immediately, and in any case within 1 hour of noticing (working hours).
Starts at once, within the first hour after the report.

Without undue delay and, where feasible, no later than 72 hours after the practice became aware of the breach (Art. 33(1) GDPR). The practice plans on the 72 hours running through weekends and days off. If the deadline is missed, the reasons for the delay are given with the notification.

deadlines.stage: Informing the people affected (if the risk is high)

deadlines.deadline: Without delay, within 24 hours of the provider becoming aware.
Within 30 days of closing the incident.

severity.description: No risk to people is likely.
severity.action: Record in the register with the reasoning. Fix the cause.

severity.description: A risk is likely, but not a high one.
severity.action: Notify the authority within 72 hours. Record. Clinic policy: also tell the people affected when health data was seen by an unauthorised person, even though the law requires this only for high risk.

severity.description: A high risk is likely (for example health data of several people exposed, or unencrypted data lost).
severity.action: Notify the authority within 72 hours and inform the people affected.

scenarios.scenario: Lab results e-mailed to another patient
scenarios.classification: Medium or high, depending on what the recipient saw. The authority is normally notified. Whether to inform the patient is assessed (often yes). Ask the recipient to delete.

scenarios.scenario: Text message with appointment details sent to a wrong number
scenarios.classification: Usually low or medium; depends on the content. Health detail raises it.

scenarios.scenario: Doctor's laptop lost or stolen, **unencrypted**, with patient data
scenarios.classification: High: authority and people. Block access and, if possible, wipe remotely.

scenarios.scenario: Same laptop, **encrypted** with a strong password; clinical data lives in the cloud application
scenarios.classification: Low or medium with reasoning; informing people is usually not needed (Art. 34(3)(a)). End the application sessions and change passwords.

scenarios.scenario: Ransomware: files encrypted, practice software unreachable
scenarios.classification: Medium or high; the authority is normally notified. If data theft is suspected, treat as high. Restore from the verified backup.

scenarios.scenario: Practice software account taken over through phishing
Staff member opens records with no care or administrative reason
scenarios.classification: Medium or high; disciplinary measures also apply.

scenarios.scenario: Paper files or lab printouts lost or stolen
scenarios.classification: Depends on how many people; health data: usually high.

scenarios.scenario: Visiting physician loses a device with his own patients' records
scenarios.classification: He is an independent controller and decides on notification; the practice helps. Arrangement to be confirmed.

scenarios.scenario: CCTV footage given to or seen by someone with no right to it
scenarios.classification: Medium; check who, what was visible, and whether the extract was logged.

scenarios.scenario: Short outage of the practice software, no data lost
scenarios.classification: Usually low, recorded; assess the effect on care.

scenarios.scenario: A provider reports a breach on its side
scenarios.classification: The practice assesses and decides on notification, because it is the controller. The 72 hours run from the provider's notice.

templates.title: Informing the people affected (Art. 34)
text: [Practice name] | [Address] | [E-mail] | [Phone]
No. [ref] / [date]
To: [Name of the person affected]
Subject: Information about a security incident involving your personal data
Dear [name],
We are writing to tell you about an incident that affected your personal data.
What happened: [clear description in simple terms: what, when, how].
What data is involved: [categories of data, without reproducing them].
What consequences may follow: [ ].
What we have done: [containment and remedy]. We have informed the National Supervisory Authority for Personal Data Processing.
What you can do: [specific advice, for example: be alert to unusual messages or calls that mention your health; do not give out passwords; contact us if you notice anything unusual].
We apologise for this. For any question, you can contact us at [contact person, phone, e-mail].

[You have the right to lodge a complaint with the National Supervisory Authority for Personal Data Processing (ANSPDCP, www.dataprotection.ro, anspdcp@dataprotection.ro) and to apply to the competent court.]
Kind regards,
[name, role]

templates.title: Request to delete a message sent to the wrong recipient
text: [Practice name] | [Address] | [E-mail] | [Phone]
No. [ref] / [date]
To: [Recipient]
Subject: Message sent in error – please delete it
Dear [name],
On [date] a message was sent to you in error by [practice name]. It contains confidential information that is not meant for you.

Please: do not read or pass on the message or its attachments; delete them permanently (including from the deleted-items folder and from any backups, if possible); and confirm to us in writing that you have done so by [date].
Thank you for your understanding, and we apologise for the inconvenience.
Kind regards,
[name, role]

registerExamples.Description (facts): Laboratory result of one patient e-mailed by the reception to a wrongly typed address, as an unprotected attachment. The unrelated recipient reported it and opened the file.
registerExamples.Consequences and measures taken: Recipient deleted the e-mail and confirmed in writing at 11:50. Password-protection and address read-back rules restated.
registerExamples.Risk (low / medium / high) and reasoning: Medium: health data seen by an unrelated person; mitigated by the recipient's prompt confirmation.
registerExamples.Authority (yes / no, date; reasoning): Yes, 9 Apr 2027, 14:30 (5 h 15 min after awareness)

registerExamples.Description (facts): Doctor's laptop left on a train. Disk encrypted, screen locked. No clinical data stored on the device: it is in the cloud application. Not recovered.
Patients: up to ~40 names on invoices
registerExamples.Consequences and measures taken: All sessions ended, passwords changed, device blocked, police report filed.
registerExamples.Risk (low / medium / high) and reasoning: Low: encrypted disk, strong password, no clinical data on the device; reasoning recorded.

registerExamples.Description (facts): Practice software unavailable for 3 hours because of a provider outage. No data lost. Paper fallback used for appointments.
registerExamples.Consequences and measures taken: Provider notice received at 09:40. Service restored at 12:00.
registerExamples.Risk (low / medium / high) and reasoning: Low: no loss, no unauthorised access; effect on care assessed as minimal.
